raw_case_text:
A 44-year-old married Acehnese man presented to the dermatology and venereology outpatient clinic of Zainoel Abidin Hospital on November 8, 2021, with the chief complaint of thick, red, scaly patches and scabs all over the body that felt itchy, especially at night. The symptoms had appeared intermittently for the last 10 years; however, the condition had worsened in the last 2 months. The initial lesions were red patches and small blisters filled with cloudy fluid that were noted on the elbow and left leg in 2011. The lesions then spread to the abdomen, buttocks, thighs, and calves, accompanied by itching at night. The patient lives with his wife and children in the same house. The patient's child also complained of itchy, red spots between the fingers, especially at night, for the last 2 months. The patient sought primary health care and was referred to a dermatologist, but the symptoms persisted. No history of diabetes mellitus, HIV/AIDS, leprosy, or other autoimmune diseases was noted. There was no history of allergies to food, drugs, or other allergens. The patient works as a bus driver and often interacts with many people. The patient has children who attend the Islamic boarding schools. The patient bathes twice daily and uses different towels than other family members. The patient's clothes were not washed separately from other family members and were washed with normal-temperature water.
Based on the physical examination, the patient was fully alert and the vital sign within normal limit. From dermatological status multiple hyperpigmented macules, erythematous papules, excoriation, erosion, scales, and crusts were generalized distributed entire the body (Figure 1). Other physical examination within normal limit. Additional examinations were performed for this patient, including a COVID-19 rapid antigen serology test with a negative result and an HIV test with non-reactive result. Skin scraping examination was performed, and Sarcoptes scabiei mites were found (Figure 2). On the 8th day of follow-up examination, several blisters were found on the leg, and on dermatological examination, we found multiple yellowish erythematous and hyperkeratotic plaques with well-defined, irregular edges of varying sizes accompanied by thick scales, vesicles, bullae, crusting, erosion, and excoriation with generalized distribution on the anterior, posterior, inferior extremity, and manus regions. Histopathological examination was performed with microscopic results of tissue preparations that revealed a stratified, encrusted epithelium with mild hyperkeratosis. In the infra-basal layer, one or two bullae were found with lymphocytes. The subepithelium contained fibromyxoid tissue. The impression of the histopathological examination was scabies bullosa (Figure 3), and pus culture analysis revealed the bacterium Kocuria kristinae, a gram-positive coccus from the Micrococcaceae family, and penicillin-class medications were recommended (Figure 4). Based on the results of supporting examinations, the diagnosis of this patient was erythroderma with Norwegian scabies and bullous scabies.    
The patient was treated with permethrin lotion 5% administered at night on days 1, 6, 9, 10, 11, and 12; mupirocin ointment 2% administered topically in the morning, afternoon, and evening; salicylic acid 3% combined with clobetasol propionate ointment applied topically during the day; and salicylic acid 3% combined with desoximetasone 0.25% ointment applied topically in the morning. Sofra-Tulle  was applied topically to areas with open, wet wounds, and salicylic acid 10% + vaseline was applied topically in the morning and evening.
As systemic treatment patient was received intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g/12 hours for 10 days, cetirizine tablet 3x50 mg orally, and ivermectin 24 mg orally on days 1, 2, 8, 9, 15, 27, and 29. After obtaining the pus culture results, clindamycin 2x300 mg was added for the treatment. After day 8, new vesicles and blisters appeared on the lower extremities, and the patient received methylprednisolone 3x8 mg/8 hours orally (Figure 5). The patient was then discharged from the hospital and continued the therapy at home. He gradually improved, with some lesions becoming dry, leaving only hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules (Figure 6). The prognosis of the patient in terms of quo ad vitam, quo ad functionam, and quo ad sanationam was dubia ad bonam.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old married Acehnese man presented with thick, red, scaly patches and scabs generalized over his body accompanied by nocturnal pruritus for 10 years, worsening over the preceding 2 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient's dermatological condition began in 2011 as erythematous patches and small cloudy fluid-filled blisters on the elbow and left leg. Over a 10-year intermittent course, the lesions spread to the abdomen, buttocks, thighs, and calves with prominent nighttime itching, and markedly worsened over the 2 months prior to presentation on November 8, 2021. Despite prior evaluation in primary care and referral to a dermatologist, his symptoms persisted.
subjective.past_medical_history: He had no history of diabetes mellitus, HIV/AIDS, leprosy, or autoimmune diseases. He worked as a bus driver with frequent public contact and lived with his wife and children (who attended Islamic boarding schools). His child had also experienced itchy erythematous spots in the finger webs, particularly at night, for the past 2 months. Although he bathed twice daily and used separate towels, his clothing was washed together with other family members' clothes in normal-temperature water.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for nocturnal pruritus; after day 8 of admission, new vesicles and blisters developed on the lower extremities. Negative for known allergies to food, drugs, or other allergens.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, the patient was fully alert with vital signs within normal limits and an unremarkable systemic physical examination. Dermatological examination revealed generalized multiple hyperpigmented macules, erythematous papules, excoriations, erosions, scales, and crusts across the entire body. On day 8 of follow-up, multiple yellowish erythematous and hyperkeratotic plaques of varying sizes with well-defined, irregular edges accompanied by thick scales, vesicles, bullae, crusting, erosions, and excoriations were noted in a generalized distribution over the anterior, posterior, inferior extremity, and manus regions.
objective.routine_investigations: COVID-19 rapid antigen serology test was negative, and HIV testing was non-reactive.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin scraping examination identified Sarcoptes scabiei mites. Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy demonstrated a stratified, encrusted epithelium with mild hyperkeratosis, one to two infra-basal bullae containing lymphocytes, and subepithelial fibromyxoid tissue.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Histopathological findings confirmed bullous scabies, skin scrapings confirmed Sarcoptes scabiei infestation, and pus culture isolated Kocuria kristinae (a gram-positive coccus of the Micrococcaceae family susceptible to penicillin-class antibiotics), establishing a final diagnosis of erythroderma secondary to Norwegian (crusted) scabies and bullous scabies with secondary bacterial infection. Topical therapy included permethrin 5% lotion applied at night (days 1, 6, 9, 10, 11, and 12), mupirocin 2% ointment three times daily, salicylic acid 3% with clobetasol propionate ointment during the day, salicylic acid 3% with desoximetasone 0.25% ointment in the morning, Sofra-Tulle dressings on open wet wounds, and salicylic acid 10% in petrolatum twice daily. Systemic treatment consisted of intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g every 12 hours for 10 days, oral cetirizine 50 mg three times daily, and oral ivermectin 24 mg on days 1, 2, 8, 9, 15, 27, and 29; oral clindamycin 300 mg twice daily was added following pus culture results, and oral methylprednisolone 8 mg three times daily (every 8 hours) was initiated after day 8 for new bullous lesions. The patient was discharged on home therapy with gradual drying and resolution of lesions into residual hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules, and a prognosis of dubia ad bonam.
